records.summary: `deacon build --label` applies the labels to the produced image on EVERY configuration shape. The reference CLI applies them on image-reference configurations and silently drops them on Dockerfile-based ones, with or without Features. Backs the scoped allowed-difference on `case-build-upstream-cli-label-dockerfile-shape`: the tolerance names the two label KEYS the flag asked for, never `chan-image.labels` as a whole.
records.rationale:
MEASURED at oracle 0.87.0 across all four `build` shapes on fresh workspaces, passing `--label name=label-test --label type=multiple-labels` to each: image-reference and image-reference-with-Features carry both labels on BOTH CLIs; `build.dockerfile` and `build.dockerfile`-with-Features carry both on deacon and NEITHER on the reference. The reference's Feature-extended Dockerfile image still carries `devcontainer.metadata`, so it is the flag's values specifically that are lost, not labelling in general; and its featureless Dockerfile image carries no labels at all.

SPEC-SILENT SURFACE, and the standing rule on those is that the reference is the authority — so this record exists to say why that rule is not being applied here rather than to quietly override it. The reference is not consistent with ITSELF: the same flag, documented by its own `--help` as additional image labels with no shape qualification, reaches the image on one configuration shape and not another. There is no answer to match, only an inconsistency to pick a side of, and the same fixture shows the reference forwarding `build.options`-supplied `--label` arguments on the very Dockerfile shape where it drops the flag's own — which is asserted, green and untoleranced by `case-build-upstream-target-and-options`. Matching would mean making a documented flag silently do nothing on the commonest configuration shape there is, the class of silent-fallback constitution IV rules out.

UNADJUDICATED — referred up rather than decided here, on the precedent of `bhv-compose-containerenv-newline-fidelity`. The evidence is complete and the tolerance is self-invalidating: it is carried by a differential case that re-measures the difference every nightly run, so if upstream ever forwards the flag on Dockerfile shapes this record fails as stale instead of silently outliving the difference.

records.summary: A `containerEnv` value containing real newlines reaches a Compose container with those newlines intact from deacon, and with each one flattened to the two-character sequence `\n` from the reference CLI.
records.rationale: Maintainer ruling on [#480](https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/480), 2026-08-22: deacon keeps its behavior, and the difference is characterized rather than matched. MEASURED four ways at oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-upstream-containerenv-dollar-escape`, whose `Test_Message` authors real newlines, reading the bytes through `od -c` and `docker inspect` in agreement — deacon delivers 0x0A on BOTH the image and the Compose path; the reference delivers 0x0A on the image path and 0x5C 0x6E on the Compose path. That asymmetry is the argument: the same CLI, given the same value, answers differently depending on which path provisions the container, so the flattening reads as an artifact of its Compose YAML serialization (the same code neighborhood as the backslash defect deacon fixed in #609) rather than a designed behavior. Matching it would mean deliberately corrupting user data — a PEM key, a multi-line banner, any authored multi-line value — on a surface the spec does not govern: `devcontainerjson-reference.md:15` defines `containerEnv` as "a set of name-value pairs that sets or overrides environment variables" and says nothing about the bytes of a value. Because the spec is silent, this is NOT recorded as deacon-follows-the-spec; it is a documented choice, made deliberately and against the reference's authority on a spec-silent surface, which is the disposition `docs/PARITY.md` reserves for the maintainer. Scoped to the one key on the one case that measures it, so any other environment difference on that fixture still fails, and the tolerance goes STALE the day the reference stops flattening — which is the mechanism by which this record retires itself.

records.summary: deacon derives a valid, deacon-namespaced, human-readable compose project name (deacon_<folderStem>_<workspaceHash>_<configHash>, falling back to deacon_<workspaceHash>_<configHash> when the stem sanitizes to empty) that docker compose always accepts and that does not collide with the reference's <folder>_devcontainer project, where the reference can emit an invalid or colliding name.
records.rationale: Robustness differentiator (issue #265; docs/DIFFERENTIATORS.md). The reference derives <folder>_devcontainer verbatim, so a folder like `-myproj` yields an invalid --project-name docker compose rejects. deacon's derived name is always valid and isolated. The workspace-folder stem leads the two hashes as of the maintainer ruling on issue #564 (2026-08-11): the hash-only form identified nothing to someone reading `docker compose ps`, and deacon's primary audience is a terminal plus a CLI-based coding agent — there is no VS Code integration path for deacon, so the both-tools-provisioning-one-workspace collision #265 defends against is a migration period rather than a steady state. Both hashes stay and both are load-bearing: workspaceHash separates two checkouts sharing a basename, configHash is what makes an edited configuration a new generation (#371, #551 depend on it). The stem is sanitized to Compose's [a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]* (lowercased, disallowed characters replaced, runs collapsed, leading non-alphanumerics trimmed, truncated to 32 characters) and an empty result falls back to the hash-only form, which is the `-myproj` case this record was written for. Explicit user declarations (COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME in a sibling .env, a compose file's top-level `name:`) still win verbatim ahead of any derivation. Because compose prefixes named volumes with the project name, the rename orphans an existing project's volumes; `up` emits a one-time diagnostic naming the project it will use when it finds this workspace's volumes under an older deacon project or under a <folder>_devcontainer project. Backed by case-up-compose-project-resources-differential, case-state-compose-feature-mounts and case-state-compose-sidecar-volume, each of which observes com.docker.compose.project and declares the name difference as a scoped tolerance rather than normalizing it away.

records.summary: When a Compose service's image is extended with Features, each CLI builds that image itself, so Compose's `com.docker.compose.image` label records a different content digest on each side.
records.rationale: Measured against oracle 0.87.0 on fx-state-compose-feature-mounts: deacon `sha256:2badca10…`, reference `sha256:35612053…`. The label carries a DIGEST of an image each side built separately from its own generated Dockerfile, so it differs by construction and can never agree — the same reason a built image's identity is not captured on `chan-image` at all. Comparing it would report a divergence on every run while saying nothing about behavior; what the two sides must agree on is what the image CONTAINS, which `env`, `user`, `workingDir` and the mount graph on this same channel do compare. Visible only when Features force a rebuild: the sibling case fx-state-compose-sidecar-volume runs the service image unmodified and this label agrees there, which is what keeps the tolerance from being a blanket excuse for the key.

records.summary: Both CLIs override the container command with a shell keep-alive that holds the container open for exec/lifecycle work and exits cleanly on SIGTERM; the command STRINGS differ. deacon uses `trap "exit 0" TERM INT; (sleep infinity || tail -f /dev/null) & wait $!`, the reference `echo Container started; trap "exit 0" 15; exec "$@"; while sleep 1 & wait $!; do :; done`.
records.rationale: Classified as intentional ONLY because the observable behavior was measured equal, not because the difference looks cosmetic. `docker stop`: deacon 245 ms (single-container) / 138 ms (compose), reference 215 ms; exit code 0 on both sides. deacon's form additionally keeps the BusyBox fallback (`sleep infinity` is rejected on Alpine) and a PATH prefix that survives a feature rewriting PATH. An EARLIER version of this same field was recorded as intentional on the assumption that a keep-alive cannot matter behaviorally — that assumption was false and hid a 10,258 ms `docker stop` stall with a SIGKILL exit (fixed in e243921, T114). The difference between then and now is that the equivalence is measured.

records.summary: deacon stamps one extra bookkeeping label, `org.deacon.configHash`, on the image a `build` produces; the reference CLI has no such label. Backs the scoped allowed-difference on the build image-discovery cases: the tolerance names that ONE key, never the `org.deacon.*` namespace.

deacon records five extra identity/bookkeeping labels on a created container (configHash, config_name, name, source, workspaceHash) that the reference CLI has no concept of. Backs the scoped allowed-differences on the chan-container-state cases: each tolerance names ONE label key, never the devcontainer.* namespace.

deacon resolves the full `extends` chain eagerly across read-configuration/up/build (merging base config, rejecting missing/cyclic targets), an ahead-of-spec capability tracking the in-flight proposal devcontainers/spec#22 that the reference CLI v0.87.0 does not implement. Recorded as an extension so the extends divergences are never misreported as parity drift.

Both CLIs layer a generated override on the workspace's Compose file and deliver it differently: deacon writes it to Compose's stdin, which Compose records as `-` in `com.docker.compose.project.config_files`; oracle 0.87.0 writes `/tmp/devcontainercli-vscode/docker-compose/docker-compose.devcontainer.containerFeatures-<id>.yml` and records that path.
records.rationale: Both CLIs layer a generated override on the workspace's Compose file and deliver it differently: deacon writes it to Compose's stdin, which Compose records as `-` in `com.docker.compose.project.config_files`; oracle 0.87.0 writes `/tmp/devcontainercli-vscode/docker-compose/docker-compose.devcontainer.containerFeatures-<id>.yml` and records that path. `com.docker.compose.config-hash` differs as a direct consequence, because Compose hashes the merged file set. Neither delivery mechanism is spec-defined and neither is observable in the container beyond these two bookkeeping labels: the service, the project-relative network and volume, the mounts and the environment are all compared and all agree. Scoped to the two derived labels by name — the project NAME difference alongside them is a separate, separately backed tolerance (`bhv-compose-project-name-robust`), because an implementation could adopt either CLI's project naming and still deliver its override the other way. ADJUDICATED 2026-08-03 and KEPT. Spec-check completed (the step the record was missing): the pinned spec defines `dockerComposeFile` purely as user input — a path or ordered list relative to devcontainer.json — and says nothing about how a tool delivers its own generated override to Compose; `com.docker.compose.project.config_files`/`config-hash` are Compose's internal bookkeeping, not spec surface. With the mechanism unspecified and every container observable measured equal (service, network, volumes, mounts, environment), the difference is delivery mechanism alone, and stdin delivery is the deliberate deacon choice (no temp file to leak).

records.summary: The residual left after #373 closed the CONTENT difference in `devcontainer.metadata` and #394 closed the KEY ORDER one: both values now record the same entries in the same authored key order, and only JSON WHITESPACE differs.
records.rationale: The residual left after #373 closed the CONTENT difference in `devcontainer.metadata` and #394 closed the KEY ORDER one: both values now record the same entries in the same authored key order, and only JSON WHITESPACE differs. WHITESPACE, measured at oracle 0.87.0: the reference emits `[ {…}, {…} ]` whenever the value reaches the container through an image build — written into a generated `LABEL` line and inherited — and compact `[{…}]` when it writes the container label directly (verified both ways). deacon always writes the container label directly, so it is always compact. Matching this would mean varying deacon's label formatting by whether an image build happened, mimicking an artifact of the reference's own build routing that no consumer can observe, since both parse to the same JSON. NARROWED BY #394, which was this record's second cause and was never an accepted difference: deacon emitted `containerEnv`/`remoteEnv` in `HashMap` iteration order, so a multi-key value was not byte-stable run to run. Both fields are `IndexMap` now, so the label records the order the author wrote and two `up` runs over one configuration produce byte-identical values — measured by `docker inspect` of the label across repeated runs, not inferred from the type change. Key order is therefore NOT tolerated here any more: should the two sides' key order diverge again, the values stop being whitespace-identical and this record no longer covers them. ADJUDICATED 2026-08-03 and KEPT, on the whitespace residual that is now this record's whole claim. The ruling argues from the evidence already above rather than from a fresh measurement, because the measurement is what settles it: the reference emits the spaced form ONLY when the value travels through an image build, so its own byte form varies with its internal build routing rather than with anything about the configuration, and once #373 closed the content and #394 closed the key order the two values parse to identical JSON with identical keys in identical order. There is therefore nothing here a consumer of the label can observe. Matching it would mean varying deacon's label formatting by whether a build happened — reproducing an artifact of the reference's routing inside a value every reader parses — which is a cost paid for no observable gain. Scoped to the one label key on the three cases where an image build makes the difference visible — `case-state-dockerfile-nonroot`, `case-up-env-merge-differential`, and `case-state-compose-feature-mounts`, where the Feature layer forces the reference to build the Compose service's image (added when #437 closed the CONTENT difference on the Compose path and left only the whitespace, verified whitespace-only on that fixture). The cases that reach this label WITHOUT an image build compare it byte-for-byte and MUST agree; their tolerances were deleted with #373 and their agreement is what proves the content fix. Self-invalidating: the moment deacon's label bytes match, this waiver reports stale.

records.summary: The spec's devcontainer-reference lists `.devcontainer/<folder>/devcontainer.json` (one level deep) as a discovery location.
records.rationale: The spec's devcontainer-reference lists `.devcontainer/<folder>/devcontainer.json` (one level deep) as a discovery location. deacon searches it; the pinned reference v0.87.0 requires an explicit --config and exits non-zero. deacon is on the spec's side, so the difference is characterized rather than followed — the waiver records that the reference is blind to a location the spec names, and self-invalidates if a later oracle starts searching it.

records.summary: JSONC with a hard syntax error.
records.rationale: JSONC with a hard syntax error. deacon rejects at parse; the reference uses a recovering jsonc parser that accepts and drops whatever follows the break. ADJUDICATED 2026-08-02 and kept, with the measurements folded in because the original two-line rationale asserted the conclusion without them. deacon is NOT stricter than the format, only strict about it — measured against oracle 0.87.0 on four documents: line and block comments ACCEPTED by both; a trailing comma ACCEPTED by both; `"features":` with no value REJECTED by deacon, accepted by the reference; an unclosed object REJECTED by deacon, accepted by the reference. Everything valid JSONC permits, deacon takes. WHAT ACCEPTANCE COSTS: in the `"features":` document the author wrote a `features` key, and the reference's resolved configuration reports only `name` and `image` — the Features are gone, with no diagnostic and exit 0; the unclosed document loses everything after the break the same way. deacon reports `JSONC parsing error: Unexpected close brace on line 5 column 1`. That is the same failure shape this project refused to ship in its own code the day this was adjudicated: the duplicate-Features fix (#430) was held back precisely because removing a validation made deacon silently drop a declared Feature, and landed on 2026-08-03 only once the whole pipeline installed both. Accepting here would put deacon on both sides of constitution IV. SPEC POSITION: devcontainer-reference.md names the format — metadata 'can be stored in a JSON with Comments file called devcontainer.json' — but says nothing about a file that is not valid JSONC, so the spec is genuinely silent and the behavior's `spec: unspecified` stands. Revisit if the spec ever defines recovery semantics for a malformed configuration, at which point deacon should follow it.

records.summary: deacon resolves the full `extends` chain before reporting Feature versions, so a Feature declared by a parent link appears in the report; the pinned reference does not implement `extends` at all and prints a header-only empty table.
records.rationale: deacon resolves the full `extends` chain before reporting Feature versions, so a Feature declared by a parent link appears in the report; the pinned reference does not implement `extends` at all and prints a header-only empty table. Part of the `ext-extends-resolution` capability — the divergence is the reference's missing feature, not deacon's drift — and the SHAPE of the miss is what makes it worth recording rather than shrugging at: the reference exits 0 on a workspace whose only Feature is declared one link up, so its user reads "nothing to report" where an outdated Feature exists. Silence is the worst answer a version report can give. RESTORED AND RE-MEASURED 2026-08-03 against oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-outdated-extends-feature`, with ONE argv driving both sides — `outdated --workspace-folder … --output-format json`, which is the reference's spelling and which deacon accepts as a visible alias for `--output` for exactly this reason (#389). deacon: `{"features":{"ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/git:1.3.2":{"current":"1.3.2","wanted":"1.3.2","latest":"1.3.8",…}}}`. Reference: `{"features":{}}`. Both exit 0. The difference still reproduces. WHY THIS RECORD CAME BACK: between #435 and now the behavior was pinned on deacon's side ALONE — a `spec-expectation` case asserts what deacon prints and never runs the reference — so nothing would have noticed the day the reference started resolving `extends`, and a one-sided pin cannot go stale because it never looks at the other side. It is now consumed by `case-outdated-extends-chain-features-differential`, scoped to the single one-sided key in the report, and self-invalidates the moment the two sides agree. Both cases stay: the pinned one gates every pull request, the differential runs nightly.

records.summary: `outdated` on a workspace whose `devcontainer-lock.json` is present but invalid: deacon exits 1 naming the file and the validation failure, the reference exits 0 with a full report because it never reads a lockfile for this subcommand.
records.rationale: deacon reads `devcontainer-lock.json` for `outdated` and lets it supply the reported `current` version; the reference CLI does not read it at all for this subcommand, so a malformed lockfile cannot affect its answer and it has nothing to reject. Measured at oracle 0.87.0 on the same workspace: deacon exits 1 naming the file and the precise validation failure, the reference exits 0 with a full report. The difference in exit code is therefore a consequence of deacon consuming an input the reference does not, not of the two disagreeing about how to treat that input. deacon fails fast per constitution IV: silently ignoring a file the author wrote, which changes the reported answer, is the worse outcome — that swallow was #406. The absent-vs-invalid distinction is preserved and separately asserted: an absent lockfile stays silent and successful, because most workspaces have none. Revisit if #407 divergence 3 resolves toward deacon dropping lockfile support in `outdated`, at which point this waiver and its behavior both go away. ADJUDICATED 2026-08-02 and KEPT. RESTORED AND RE-MEASURED 2026-08-03 against oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-outdated-malformed-lockfile` (`resolved` is `"x"`, not an OCI digest reference): deacon exit 1 — `Failed to read lockfile at '…/devcontainer-lock.json'` / `Invalid resolved field for feature 'ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/git': OCI reference 'x' must contain '@' separator with digest` — against the reference's exit 0 and `{"features":{"ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/git:1":{"current":"1.3.8",…}}}`. The difference still reproduces. WHY THIS RECORD CAME BACK: the ruling kept it, but between #435 and now it was enforced by nothing — the `spec-expectation` case pins deacon's exit 1 and never runs the reference, so a tolerance that could go stale did not exist and the record read as characterized coverage nothing exercised (#423). It is now consumed by `case-outdated-malformed-lockfile-rejected-differential` on `chan-exit-code.exitCode`, the one path where the difference is addressable, and self-invalidates if the two exit codes ever converge. Both cases stay: the pinned one gates every pull request, the differential runs nightly.

records.summary: Surfaced by the 024 US5 de-suppression, which narrowed `drop_absent_optional` to deacon's side.
records.rationale: Surfaced by the 024 US5 de-suppression, which narrowed `drop_absent_optional` to deacon's side. While the rule ran on BOTH sides, an authored null, an authored empty collection and an omitted property all normalized to 'the key is absent on both sides', so the three FR-055 states produced ONE observation and the difference could not be seen. SHRUNK BY #398, which wrapped every modeled optional — including the eleven properties previously typed as bare collections — in `Option` with `skip_serializing_if`. Re-measured at oracle 0.87.0 on `fx-us5-null-empty-omitted`: `configuration.forwardPorts`, `configuration.containerEnv` and `nullEmptyOmitted.mounts` now AGREE, so their tolerances were DELETED rather than narrowed — a tolerance whose difference stopped reproducing is stale by design, and leaving it would suppress the next real difference on that path. WHAT IS STILL TOLERATED is the authored `"name": null`, on the raw key and on the derived FR-055 classification: deacon holds an authored null and an omission in the same `None`, so omitting unauthored optionals necessarily omits authored nulls too. That boundary MOVED rather than closed — before the fix both CLIs emitted `null` here and AGREED — which the pre-#398 version of this waiver predicted in as many words. Net: deacon went from ~40 unconditionally emitted keys to the 2 the reference emits for a minimal configuration, and the residual is one schema-invalid input shape. This remains a fidelity DEFECT, not a design choice, tracked at #398 with the remaining scope named there. Scoped to the named paths on the one case authored to demonstrate them; self-invalidates the moment a difference stops reproducing. ADJUDICATED 2026-08-03: the residual is NOT OWED and the record is KEPT as a documented choice, superseding the earlier 'fix deacon' ruling whose fixable half #398 already closed. Measured at oracle 0.87.0 (#398 residual investigation): the reference preserves an authored `null` on EVERY property because its read-configuration echoes the parsed document verbatim — deacon drops it on every Option<T> field, flattens it inside nested structs, and REJECTS it on the strict object fields via deserialize_object_value. Reaching parity would require a whole-struct three-state change plus reversing that deliberate strictness for a schema-invalid value — the same lenient-echo-versus-eager-validation axis already characterized by the bhv-readconfig-* rejection family (constitution IV, fail fast). The residual is that family's shape, not a fidelity gap deacon owes.

records.summary: Made visible by #398 rather than caused by it.
records.rationale: Made visible by #398 rather than caused by it. `mergedConfiguration` is SYNTHESIZED by both CLIs, so an empty value there is a computed default rather than authorship information — which is exactly why `drop_absent_optional` still runs on BOTH sides of that block and why #398 retired it only on `configuration`. Until #398, deacon emitted its own empties there too and the rule absorbed the difference symmetrically; now deacon omits them and the reference does not, so the difference has a direction and is recorded here instead of being only compensated. Measured at oracle 0.87.0 for `{"image": "alpine:3.19"}`: the reference emits `remoteEnv: {}`, `containerEnv: {}`, `portsAttributes: {}` and `hostRequirements: {cpus: null, memory: "-Infinity", storage: "-Infinity"}`; deacon emits none of the four. The two documents describe the same merged configuration — no consumer can act differently on an absent `containerEnv` than on an empty one — so the divergence is tolerated rather than treated as a defect to rush a fix for. The `hostRequirements` values in particular are upstream's `Math.max()` over an empty set serialized as the strings `"-Infinity"`, and reproducing that shape uncritically would be adopting a quirk, not achieving parity. Self-invalidates the moment the difference stops reproducing. ADJUDICATED 2026-08-03 and KEPT. Spec-check completed: image-metadata.md's merge-logic table defines HOW each property merges (`hostRequirements`: 'Max value wins') and says nothing about emitting a property with ZERO contributions — and 'max over an empty set' is precisely where the reference's `-Infinity` comes from, a value that is itself INVALID by the spec's own format for `hostRequirements.memory` ('a string with a tb/gb/mb/kb suffix'). Reproducing a spec-invalid value would be adopting a bug, not achieving parity. Enforcement is live via case-readconfig-merged-computed-empties (#423), scoped to the one observable path.

records.summary: Discovered by the 024 US4 error-path tier, which compares past the point where configuration read accepts on both sides.
records.rationale: Discovered by the 024 US4 error-path tier, which compares past the point where configuration read accepts on both sides. `run-user-commands` re-runs the configured lifecycle commands on EVERY invocation in deacon; the reference records each hook's completion inside the container and skips one that already completed, reporting `{"outcome":"success"}` without running anything. Verified directly at oracle 0.87.0: after `devcontainer up`, a plain `devcontainer run-user-commands` does not re-run `postCreateCommand`, while after `devcontainer up --skip-post-create` it does — so the skip is keyed on completion, not on the command being absent. The observable consequence is confined to a FAILING hook: deacon exits non-zero and names the hook, the reference exits 0 having executed nothing, so the same broken setup is invisible on its side. deacon's direction is the one that keeps `run-user-commands` usable as an explicit re-run (its `--skip-post-create` / `--skip-post-attach` / `--skip-non-blocking-commands` flags are the opt-out, so silence would leave no way to ask for the work), and it is the direction the spec's account of lifecycle-command failure supports. Pinned in that direction by the `-direction` spec-expectation twins rather than by this waiver alone: a differential shows only that the two disagree.

records.summary: deacon validates modelled fields against the pinned schema's closed enums during configuration resolution; the reference's read-configuration is a lenient parse-and-echo that accepts and prints the value back.
records.rationale: deacon validates modelled fields against the pinned schema's closed enums during configuration resolution; the reference's read-configuration is a lenient parse-and-echo that accepts and prints the value back. This tolerance absorbs the REFERENCE's departure from the schema — bhv-readconfig-unsupported-enum-rejected is `follow-spec`, so nothing here waives a deacon deviation. It exists because the live-differential case would otherwise fail on a difference we expect to keep seeing, and it self-invalidates the day the reference starts validating.

records.summary: Re-entering a workspace whose configuration has CHANGED since its container was created: deacon provisions a new container for the new configuration, the reference reattaches to the container built from the old one.
records.rationale: Surfaced by the 024 US3 stale-config re-entry case. Re-entering a workspace whose configuration has CHANGED since its container was created: the reference reattaches to the existing container, deacon provisions a new one. Measured directly at oracle 0.87.0 against `fx-up-stale-config` — two `up` runs whose documents differ only in `name` and `containerEnv.CONF_GENERATION` return the IDENTICAL containerId from `devcontainer up` and two different containerIds from `deacon up`. deacon is the stricter side and deliberately so: its container identity includes a configHash (`ext-container-identity-labels`, a label the reference does not set), so a changed document is a different identity. Reattaching is the dangerous branch — the container keeps the Feature layer built from the OLD configuration while every reported value comes from the NEW one — which is the failure the recreate avoids. SPEC POSITION, stated against the strongest text rather than around it: devcontainer-reference.md §Environment Resume covers resuming from a STOPPED state and says nothing about a configuration that has changed, so there is no re-entry policy to follow. The nearest passage cuts the other way and is cited here so the record does not read as if it did not exist — feature-dependencies.md §Image Metadata: 'For subsequent creations from an image (or resumes of a dev container), the dependency tree is not re-calculated. To re-calculate the dependency tree, the user must delete the image (or dev container) and recreate it from a devcontainer.json.' That describes resumption REUSING, and puts the recreate burden on the user, which is nearer the reference's reattach than to deacon's automatic recreate. It is descriptive of dependency-tree recalculation rather than a MUST about re-entry, so it does not make deacon nonconformant and the spec axis stays unspecified; but it is the strongest spec text bearing on this choice, and a reader weighing the record deserves to see it. The argument for recreating is a safety one, not a spec one: the passage assumes the configuration is unchanged, and says nothing about the case where it is not — which is precisely where reattaching serves a container built from a document that no longer exists. Tracked separately and never waived, because it was a bug rather than a choice: deacon LEFT the superseded container running, so one workspace ended up with two live containers (https://github.com/get2knowio/deacon/issues/371). FIXED 2026-08-07 — a superseded container is now stopped (not removed, per the maintainer ruling, so its state and volumes survive for `docker start` recovery). The recreate was the decision; the leak was a defect, and keeping the two apart is why this waiver never covered it. ADJUDICATED 2026-08-02 and KEPT. RESTORED AND RE-MEASURED 2026-08-03 against oracle 0.87.0: the reference returned `e98be9c32a41…` from BOTH runs, deacon `d796c31240e5…` then `32ae762fd677…`. The difference still reproduces, and this restoration is what finally makes it OBSERVABLE rather than asserted. A container id is incomparable across the two sides by construction — each CLI creates its own — so the recreate/reattach split has to be read from what it COSTS. Reading it from the created container looked right and was not usable at the time: both generations carry the workspace label, and while both were RUNNING (#371) which one the probe observed was a coin flip on their hex ids. #371 settled that — one generation is live and the runner observes the running container — but the host-marker read is kept, because it does not depend on the probe's choice at all. It is read instead from the workspace, where a lifecycle hook leaves a trace the host can see: each generation of the configuration appends its name from `postCreateCommand`, and `postCreate` runs on CREATE. deacon's `generations.txt` reads `first\nsecond`; the reference's reads `first`, because nothing was created and the new document's work never happened. That is the waiver's own safety argument, measured. WHY THIS RECORD CAME BACK: the ruling kept it, but between #435 and now it was enforced by nothing — the `spec-expectation` case pins deacon's recreate and never runs the reference (#423). It is now consumed by `case-up-stale-config-reentry-differential` on the one file its fixture writes, and self-invalidates the moment the two sides converge. Both cases stay: the pinned one gates every pull request, the differential runs nightly.
